output.query: timing of anticoagulation after acute ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation

results.authors: Fischer U, Koga M, Strbian D, et al.
results.key_finding: Early DOAC initiation (within 48 hours after a minor or moderate stroke, on day 6 or 7 after a major stroke, by imaging size) had a 30-day composite of recurrent ischaemic stroke, systemic embolism, major bleeding, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage or vascular death of 2.9% versus 4.1% with later initiation; symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0.2% in both groups.
results.title: Early versus Later Anticoagulation for Stroke with Atrial Fibrillation (ELAN)

results.authors: Werring DJ, Dehbi HM, Ahmed N, et al.
results.key_finding: DOAC initiation within 4 days of onset was non-inferior to delayed initiation at 7 to 14 days for recurrent stroke, symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism at 90 days.
results.title: Optimal timing of anticoagulation after acute ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation (OPTIMAS)

output.summary: Randomised trials show that early DOAC initiation after atrial fibrillation-related ischaemic stroke, timed by infarct size, is not associated with more haemorrhage than later initiation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis while blood pressure is 185/110 mmHg or higher.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000, there was recent major surgery, or another guideline-listed contraindication is present.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or laboratory results in a stroke alert.
Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.
Do not start anticoagulation within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis or before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation, and do not bridge with heparin.
Do not use diltiazem or verapamil for rate control in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:00, 2 hours 28 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (16).

IV thrombolysis: give once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (2 hours 28 minutes from last known well; warfarin stopped 3 weeks ago and INR 1.2, below 1.7; platelets 216). Thrombectomy: proceed for the proximal left M1 occlusion (NIHSS 16, independent before the stroke, ASPECTS 10, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg (190/100 on arrival) with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; after successful recanalization do not target systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.

Proceed with CTA without waiting for creatinine; a prior mild contrast reaction and CKD stage 3a do not justify delaying vessel imaging. Give premedication only if it causes no delay, and have treatment for a reaction at hand.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.
Control the ventricular rate of atrial fibrillation (108 bpm on arrival, daytime rates above 110 bpm on monitoring) by continuing carvedilol once swallowing is safe, avoiding hypotension.

Repeat troponin and review the ECG; the mild elevation (troponin I 0.08 ng/mL) is most likely demand ischaemia from rapid atrial fibrillation or neurogenic myocardial injury; it does not delay reperfusion.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 5; HAS-BLED 2 for uncontrolled hypertension and this stroke; no dose-reduction criterion) on day 6 to 7 for this major infarct, once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation; do not bridge with heparin.
Address why he stopped warfarin (bruising): bruising is not a reason to stop anticoagulation, and a DOAC carries a lower intracranial bleeding risk than warfarin; involve his daughter in adherence.
Intensify lipid lowering (LDL 139 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg) to an LDL below 70 mg/dL, with rosuvastatin 40 mg or added ezetimibe, for carotid atherosclerosis and diabetes.

A normal non-contrast CT under 3 hours does not exclude infarction; the MRI shows DWI restriction without FLAIR change, as expected in the hyperacute window.
A prior mild contrast reaction and CKD stage 3a do not justify delaying CTA in a thrombectomy candidate.
Atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation with heart failure, hypertension and diabetes (CHA2DS2-VASc 5) is the mechanism (TOAST cardioembolism); the echocardiogram shows no left ventricular thrombus.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: Self-discontinuation of anticoagulation is a common real-world scenario leading to cardioembolic stroke; always inquire about medication adherence
In patients with CKD, apixaban is often preferred because it depends least on renal clearance among the DOACs (about 27% renal elimination)
Spontaneous echo contrast ('smoke') in the left atrium on echocardiography indicates blood stasis and markedly elevated thromboembolic risk
The ELAN trial supports DOAC initiation within 48 hours after minor or moderate infarcts and on day 6 or 7 after major infarcts, earlier than the traditional 14-day wait

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Pradeep Singh is a 55-year-old right-handed South Asian man with a history of atrial fibrillation (previously on warfarin, self-discontinued 3 weeks ago), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and chronic kidney disease who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after the acute onset of right-sided weakness and speech difficulties. The daughter reports that his brother spoke to him on the phone at approximately 09:00 this morning and he sounded completely normal, discussing plans for a church event this weekend. The daughter stopped by to drop off groceries at 10:45 and found him sitting on the kitchen floor, leaning against the refrigerator, with his right arm limp and speech garbled. The patient was able to say 'help' and 'arm' but could not form complete sentences. He appeared to have been attempting to reach the phone. There was a broken coffee mug on the floor beside him. The daughter immediately called 911. EMS arrived at 11:02 and documented right facial droop, right upper and lower extremity weakness, and expressive aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Field glucose was 142 mg/dL. The patient was transported to our comprehensive stroke center, arriving at 11:28. On the cardiac monitor he was found to be in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 108 bpm. His blood pressure was 190/100 mmHg. He was anxious, tearful, and attempting to speak but producing only fragments and paraphasic errors. When asked why he stopped his warfarin, his daughter explained that he had noticed large bruises on his arms and legs over the past month and decided on his own to stop the medication without consulting his physician. There is no history of recent head trauma, seizure, fever, or new headache. His last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 28 minutes before ED arrival.
